scav

how a statechart gets laid out
    Introduction

    What scav is

    scav lays out and renders Harel statecharts: every state boxed, every transition routed at right angles, every label placed, identical bytes everywhere.

    Existing tools fail on what statecharts have and flowcharts lack: transitions that cross the borders of nested states.

    • ELK either drops an edge that skips a containment level, or lays the whole subtree out in one run and loses each subtree's own direction and aspect.
    • PlantUML, whose files scav replaces, lays each composite out alone and attaches leaving transitions afterwards, so its lines cut through boxes; it cannot express tcp.scav at all.
    • Of about twenty other tools surveyed, none publishes a statechart layout algorithm.

    scav's answer is decomposition: every transition is cut at each border it crosses into segments, joined by ports. Each submachine becomes a flat graph laid out on its own, and a long transition still lands in the right place because its pieces are tied to the borders.

    The model

    • A state may hold submachines of further states. With one or more it is composite; with two or more it is concurrent, and its submachines (regions) run together, drawn side by side with a dashed divider.
    • Every kind but Normal is a pseudostate: initial, final, choice, junction, fork, join, history, deep history. trans * -> X creates an initial and trans X -> * a final. Layout draws a pseudostate as a small box at its kind's minimum size: on the readable profile, 224 × 224 grid units for initial or final, 320 × 320 for a choice, 64 × 960 for a fork or join bar.
    • A transition joins any two states. If its ends lie in different submachines it is hierarchy-crossing. A transition between two regions of one state is drawn directly, not through the parent: scav draws topology, not execution paths.
    • The model is flat arrays of records, each traceable to its source statement.

    Transition kinds

    A transition's kind decides whether its arrow crosses the source's border.

    kindthe source's bordera self-transition
    external (default)crosseda loop outside the box
    internalnot crossed: the route starts on its inner facea loop inside the box
    localas internala loop inside the box

    When the destination encloses the source, the route ends on the destination's inner face, whatever the kind.

    The .scav format

    • Keyword-led, LL(1), whitespace-insensitive; commas separate items; an unnamed string after a state or transition is its label. s, m and t abbreviate state, submachine and trans.
    • States written directly in a state's block form an unnamed submachine; submachine water { … } names one region.
    • Paths are /-separated and resolve innermost-outward; :name picks a submachine, as in Brewing:water/Heating.
    • include "axis.scav" as arm makes a state arm holding the included document; each include is an independent copy.
    • scav fmt is the one canonical printer. JSON is an output, not a format.

    Layout is a library

    scav owns the model, the layout, and what layout and drawing must agree on: the draw list, space requests and text metrics. The application owns appearance and the render loop. The interface is a flat extern "C" ABI with no callbacks, shipped as libscav with Python bindings; its main user is a build system running scav render, scav fmt --check and scav check.

    Layout's only inputs are the model, a profile of 52 integer settings, and three tables of space requests. It never sees a font or a string.

    • BoxSpace, per state and submachine: the width its text needs, and four bands around its children: above, below, before and after.
    • PathClear, per transition: how far to shorten each end for the arrowhead.
    • PathBox, zero or more per transition: a label box to place along the route.

    The application measures its text with scav's metrics, fills the tables, and calls scav_layout_run, which rejects bad input rather than clamping it. It draws the returned geometry with scav's SVG back end or its own.

    ScaleThe design target is 2,000 states, 5,000 transitions and nesting 16 deep. The examples here are twelve hand-written charts, from the 3-state estop to bottler, nested six deep.
    Principles

    The rules everything else obeys

    A drawing is a pure function of chart, space requests and profile, computed in integers, so the same inputs give the same bytes everywhere.

    A pure function

    Layout reads (model, space requests, profile) and nothing else: no warm start from a previous layout, no persisted cache, no quick mode. scav does keep memos, but each is keyed on every value its step reads, so a hit returns exactly what the computation would; like the thread count, a memo changes only the wall clock.

    Stability comes from construction, not memory: each stage preserves order, every tie is broken by a total order, and document order drives reading order. A small edit can still cascade; the remedy is an author's pin, not a memory of the last layout.

    The integer grid

    All layout arithmetic is integer, because floating point and libm differ between platforms.

    • Coordinates are int32 grid units of 1/16 pt, within |x| ≤ COORD_MAX = 524,287, symmetric so negation and mirroring cannot overflow; products are int64. Space requests and spacing fields are capped at COORD_MAX / 4, since the box formula adds several.
    • Rectangles are half-open, [x0, x1) × [y0, y1).
    • Square roots use an integer isqrt, ratios are compared by cross-multiplying, and intersection tests use orient2d signs, never a constructed point.

    The 2,000-state stress chart fits about 3× inside the domain; if charts outgrow it, the grid coarsens to 1/8 pt rather than widening the integers.

    The determinism contract

    Any conforming C++20 toolchain must produce the same bytes; determinism shows how that is tested. Four rules make it hold:

    • The thread count never reaches the output. Work is cut into shards whose count depends only on the model. One process-wide pool runs them: the first free thread takes the lowest unclaimed shard of the deepest open job. Each shard writes its own slot, and results merge in index order.
    • Reductions are associative, such as argmin(value, index); saturating addition is banned because it is not.
    • Every comparator is a total order, and every sort that reaches the output is stable; std::sort is banned.
    • No randomness in layout or search. Constructs whose behaviour varies by platform are banned: variable-width integers in values, std::hash, iterating unordered containers, pointer keys, <random>, <cmath>, / and % on negatives, locale formatting, bitfields.

    Two measurement scales

    scav's numbers come in two scales that are never compared. No-text means no space requests (every state at minimum size, no labels); the cost goldens and unit tests use it. Real text means text measured with the bundled font; rendering and every other drawing on this page use it. Text changes sizes, label terms and the search's choices, so a number carried across scales checks nothing.

    RuleWhat is trivially right is built in, not left to the search: a straight line beats a kinked one, a start state sits beside the state it enters, a route never runs along a border. Every rule gets an isolated test on a trivial layout.
    Overview

    The pipeline at a glance

    Four phases (decompose, order, size, route) turn a chart into a drawing; a search reruns the last three with different choices and keeps the cheapest.

    Each phase hands the next a plain struct and never reads what an earlier phase computed from anywhere else, so a unit test can type a phase's input in directly.

    stageproduces
    0 · decomposeevery transition cut into segments at the borders it crosses, with a port at each crossing
    1 · orderper frame: each node's rank and position within it; long edges chained; label room charged to the gaps
    2 · sizeevery state and submachine rectangle, folded and packed bottom-up
    facing passports turned toward their route's far end; if any turned, phases 1 and 2 run again
    3 · routeorthogonal polylines and port positions, then placed labels
    cover and costthe chart rectangle grown over every route and label, then the Cost

    One pass from ordering through cost, for one setting of the search's choices, is a candidate. Phase 1 reads no sizes from the profile, so its first run happens once per layout and is shared by all 16 Level 2 rows and every inflation retry. A candidate with a new pin (a choice the search fixes, such as a state's rank) re-derives only what the pin reaches and copies the rest.

    The search around it

    1. Validate the profile, space tables and router name; reject on failure.
    2. Decompose and order once.
    3. Level 2: lay out 16 rows in parallel, each a whole-chart setting of four sizing knobs.
    4. Level 1, from every viable row: steepest descent over pins, one move per round, until nothing improves.
    5. Kicks: structural changes, each searched to convergence and kept only if the result is cheaper; then a refold search.
    6. Ship the cheapest row (ties to the lower row) with its geometry, labels and diagnostics.

    On mill, the largest example, one layout scores 1.6 to 1.9 million candidates; the search and making it fast explain how.

    When routing fails

    If a net is unreachable, the inflation retry widens spacing and reruns phases 2 and 3, up to 8 times. Anything still unroutable is drawn as a straight line with a RouteDegraded diagnostic; the run still succeeds.

    Phase 0

    Decompose: frames, segments, ports

    Every transition is cut at each border it crosses, leaving one flat graph per submachine, joined to the others only at ports.

    A frame is one submachine laid out as its own layered graph: a region, a composite's submachine, or a document root. It is the unit that is ordered, sized, run in parallel and reused between candidates. In its parent's frame, a composite state is a plain node.

    A transition whose ends lie in different frames is split at every border it crosses. Each piece is a segment in exactly one frame; each cut is a port on the crossed state's border. Long hierarchical edges become a matter of ordering ports along each composite's sides, and a long edge pulls on every level it passes, with no weight needed.

    How a transition is split

    1. Skip dead transitions.
    2. List each end's ancestors, innermost first, and strip the part they share.
    3. If the source encloses the destination, an internal or local transition starts on the source's inner face; an external one leaves the source and re-enters it.
    4. Exit the source's chain, innermost first; the source itself is exited only by an external transition.
    5. If the chains diverge into two submachines of one state, cross the separator between those regions instead of the state's border; that middle segment is routed in the source region's frame.
    6. Enter the destination's chain, outermost first. If the destination encloses the source, end on its inner face.
    7. Emit one port per crossing and one segment per consecutive pair of ends, each in the frame it lies in.

    A self-transition is one segment in its state's parent frame. An external one is routed there; an internal or local one is drawn as a loop inside its state and never routed.

    Each segment end is a port, an endpoint state's box, or an endpoint's inner face. In ordering, each port on a frame's border becomes a boundary node: exits on the trailing edge, entries on the leading one.

    A transition's label belongs to the segment in its lowest common ancestor (LCA) frame, the innermost submachine holding both ends; an internal or local self-transition's label sits beside its loop instead. Ports and segments have stable ids derived from the model, never from how work was split.

    RuleCutting at borders keeps each submachine independently orderable and keeps every long edge, which ELK's two modes cannot do together. Phase 0 records what kind each segment end is; later phases never infer it.
    Phase 1

    Ordering: which rank, which slot

    Phase 1 gives every node in a frame a rank (its column) and a slot within that rank.

    A frame's graph has a state node per child state in document order, a boundary node per port or inner-face end, and the bend nodes chaining adds; each segment is one edge, and self-loops are dropped. Ranks run left to right, rank_sep (576) apart, with nodes node_sep (288) apart within a rank. Ordering treats the frame as one graph, disconnected components included; sizing splits the components and packs them.

    Breaking cycles

    Layering needs an acyclic graph, and statecharts are full of cycles.

    1. Tarjan's strongly connected components mark every segment on a cycle as cyclic; only these can be reversed by the search.
    2. Every reverse pin flips its segment.
    3. A depth-first search, roots in document order and out-edges in segment order, flips every back edge (an edge into a node still on the stack). Only edge directions change.
    RuleWhich edge of a cycle is reversed is an artefact of declaration order, so reversal is a search dimension, not a rule.

    Ranking by longest path

    1. Topological order by Kahn's algorithm, sources in node order.
    2. Longest path: every edge v → w sets rank[w] = max(rank[w], rank[v] + 1).
    3. Pull right, in reverse order: a node with fewer in-edges than out-edges moves to one rank before its nearest successor, so a source sits next to its successors rather than at rank 0.
    4. Sink exit boundary nodes to the last rank, then squeeze out empty ranks.

    Pins

    • A rank pin overwrites one state's rank afterwards, without rerunning longest path, so edges may go flat or backward. Initials are never pinned: each is re-seated one rank before the state it enters (shifting the others if that state is at rank 0), and empty ranks are squeezed out.
    • A side pin on a top or bottom border takes the port's edge out of ranking and sweeps, placing it in its mate's rank; on a left or right border it orients the edge so the port is a source or a sink.

    Charging label room

    Before chaining, each gap between ranks is charged with the room it must hold, in three passes:

    1. Labels across one gap: an edge crossing one gap charges it its label's width.
    2. Lane estimate: within each connected component, every edge counts as turning in the first and last gap it crosses. A gap where two or more turn reserves one line height (269) per edge. This is an upper bound; sizing counts the edges that really turn.
    3. Labels across several gaps, widest label first: each charges the widest gap it crosses, counting the lane estimate, with ties to the middle.

    Each charge is a maximum, so a label no wider than its gap's label charge adds nothing. Sizing spaces the ranks by the label charges; folding also counts the lane estimate. scav widens gaps instead of adding a dummy node per label, which would double every rank.

    Chaining long edges

    An edge spanning several ranks becomes a chain through one bend node per intermediate rank. Bend nodes are ordered like any node, and the router treats them as hard waypoints. A cut pin leaves the edge unchained, for the router to draw freely; this matters because chained edges carry 70% of the kinks.

    Crossing minimisation by median sweeps

    Starting from document order (pinned-first ports, states, boundary nodes, bends, pinned-last ports), up to 8 sweeps reorder each rank by its nodes' neighbour positions, alternating down (by predecessors) and up (by successors).

    • A node's key is the upper median of its neighbours' positions; a node with no neighbours on that side keeps its slot.
    • Adjacent nodes swap only while strictly out of order, so ties keep their order.
    • Crossings are recounted after each sweep (by counting inversions); the best arrangement is kept, and sweeping stops at zero.

    The median has a constant-factor quality bound that the barycenter heuristic lacks. In practice every frame in the corpus ends with zero layered crossings: the crossings a reader sees come from routing.

    Orientation and fold pins

    An orient pin, applied by a kick, turns a frame to run down: ranks become rows. A fold pin passes through untouched; it tells sizing where to cut a long run of ranks.

    The real ranks

    brew's shipped pins include one rank pin and an orient pin that turns its root frame to run down; the depth-first search reverses two edges itself.

    Most of the search's moves act here: rank, cut, reverse, side and orient pins. Position within a rank is not searched; measured, it has no slack.

    RejectedGreedy cycle removal (the search chooses reversals); dot's edge-weight schedule; adjacent-swap refinement (transpose), which found nothing to improve.
    Phase 2

    Sizing: coordinates, gaps, folds and packing

    Phase 2 turns ranks and slots into rectangles, bottom-up from the deepest frames to the root.

    The deepest frames are sized first, then their owner states, then those states' frames, up to the root; one final pass makes every coordinate root-absolute. So a leaf growing one unit resizes every ancestor.

    Across the ranks: Brandes–Köpf

    Each node's coordinate across the ranks comes from Brandes–Köpf (BK), a linear-time, balanced placement, run per connected component and fold piece with node_sep between neighbours. A labelled leg adds room for its label to its node's extent.

    1. Mark conflicts: an edge crossing a chain of bend nodes is marked, so long chains stay straight.
    2. Align four ways (layers forward or backward, each from its first or last node): each node joins its median neighbour into a block sharing one coordinate, unless the edge is marked or crosses an earlier alignment. Initials' edges align last, and a segment aligns where it meets a port, not at the composite's centre.
    3. Compact each block to its coordinate, following the 2020 erratum to the published algorithm.
    4. Balance: align the four results to the narrowest, and give each node the average of its two median values.

    Then three alignment rules: states joined inside one column share a centre line; a state joined to a port is centred on it; an initial or final sits rank_sep from its mate, level with it.

    Along the ranks: gaps

    Each layer starts where the previous one ends, plus a gap:

    gap = sep + max(label charge, lanes)

    sep is rank_sep, or only the route clearance next to a layer holding just boundary nodes or seated pseudostates when no label is charged to the gap. The label charge comes from ordering. lanes is zero when fewer than two edges turn in the gap, otherwise one line height per turning edge. An edge whose ends overlap runs straight and does not turn.

    Folding long rank runs

    A long run of ranks can be folded: cut into pieces that are packed like rectangles, so a deep chain does not become one very wide strip.

    • The target width is the square root of the run's area scaled to the desired aspect ratio (DAR), at least the widest layer.
    • Cut where the running width passes the target, or at a fold pin, but never between a pseudostate or boundary node and the node it joins.
    • Keep the best of three by the scale measure (unless the frame's fold rule is Always or Never): unfolded, pieces packed, or pieces stacked. A fold whose pieces pack back into one row is not taken, and a frame running down never folds.
    • The charge on a gap a cut falls in, less node_sep, moves to the new piece's leading edge.
    The scale measureSM = min(dar_num / (dar_den · w), 1 / h): how large the drawing could be scaled in a viewport of the desired aspect. Larger wins; ties go to the smaller area, then the closer aspect.

    Packing

    Packing places a frame's components, a fold's pieces, and a concurrent state's regions (sub_sep apart). States inside a frame are layered, never packed.

    • LR-rectpacking (Domrös et al.) gives each rectangle, in order, the first of four spots beside its predecessor that stays within the target width: Level, Right, Subrow, Row. Reading order is placement order.
    • Compaction (a Level 2 knob) lets each rectangle take another spot if the result is tighter and no extent grows.
    • Whitespace elimination grows rectangles to fill their rows; extents do not change.
    • The one-row box packer is also tried when the profile's trybox is set, and wins if it scales larger.

    A packing aims at the profile's DAR (16:10 on readable) or, on some Level 2 rows, at the owner state's interior. A packing that would exceed COORD_MAX never displaces one that fits.

    Bottom-up to the root

    A composite's box wraps its packed submachines, its four bands and its loop room:

    w = max(min_w, w_before + max(packed_w, loop_w) + w_after, kind_min_w) + 2·pad
    h = max(h_before + packed_h + sep + loop_h + h_after, kind_min_h) + 2·pad

    The h_* and w_* terms are the bands the application requested above, below, before and after the submachine area. The loop room, loop_w × loop_h, holds the state's internal self-transitions, one row each, below its submachines; sep is sub_sep when both are present, else 0. pad (128) is the interior ring. A bare pseudostate has none, so an arrow stops on its mark. A plain state is at least 896 × 640 on readable; pseudostate minimums are in the model.

    After routing, the chart rectangle grows over every route point and label before scoring, so area and aspect price the canvas that ships.

    RejectedTop-down sizing (its size estimate is unsolved, and per-level scaling breaks port continuity); constraint-based adjustment (coordinates are generated, not adjusted); network-simplex placement (no fewer visible defects, and slower).
    Phase 3

    Routing: ports, faces, A*, seats and lanes

    Phase 3 draws every segment as an axis-aligned polyline; states are obstacles, so a route through a box cannot be represented at all.

    Each segment becomes a net. Every net's ends are seated, then frames are routed in parallel (a frame that has not changed reuses its previous answer), nets are joined into transitions, ends are trimmed for arrowheads, parallel lanes are nudged apart, and labels are placed last.

    Ports and the facing pass

    A port slot is where a route crosses a composite's border. In a frame running left to right, ports on the left are sources and on the right sinks; ports may also sit on the top or bottom. Sides are numbered 0 left, 1 right, 2 top, 3 bottom.

    After the first sizing, the facing pass turns ports toward their route's far end, then reruns ordering and sizing if any turned:

    • a port whose far end lies on the frame's other side has its edge reversed, moving it to the opposite border;
    • a port on its own transition's state whose far end lies further away across the ranks than along them moves to the top or bottom border facing it, if that border is unobstructed and free. A side pin is never turned;
    • a port on a lined face, one that a band of its state covers, moves to the opposite border, else to a top or bottom border its joined state can see. No port is ever turned onto a lined face.

    Which face an end leaves by

    The separation rule seats each end on a face of its box: the axis on which the far end lies further outside the box wins (a tie goes to x), and the nearer border on that axis is the face. The seat is the far end's projection onto the face, held off the corners. Inscribed glyphs (discs, diamonds) take the face's midpoint.

    A face pin overrides the rule at one end, unless the face is too short to hold a seat. Choosing both faces as a pair was tried and made most charts worse, so the face is a search dimension, not a rule.

    The orthogonal router

    The router runs A* on a separated orthogonal visibility graph:

    • Grid: lines through every obstacle edge grown by the clearance, every wall and every route end; an edge is passable unless it enters a grown obstacle. A frame over 218 vertices is refused.
    • Clearance is a bumper, not a penalty: no route comes within clear = node_sep / 3 (96) of a box, by construction.
    • Two planes: each vertex has a horizontal and a vertical copy, joined by an edge costing the bend penalty (one rank_sep), so plain A* minimises length and bends together. A turn at a fixed end costs slightly less, so equal paths turn at their ends.
    • Deterministic: the heuristic is admissible, and the open list is totally ordered by (f, g, node), so the result never depends on the queue. The search is capped at 220 expansions.
    • Ring points: an end is pushed out by the clearance, and the leg back to the box is emitted, not searched, so it is perpendicular for free.

    A chained segment's bend nodes are waypoints the route must pass, leg by leg. Each frame's obstacles are its live states except the ones the route lives inside, plus the bands and loop rooms of those it lives inside; walls keep a route inside the state it is drawn in.

    Seating passes

    Every seat is chosen before any net is searched, because two ends wanting one seat is a question about the pair. Six passes run in order:

    1. Attach: seat each end by the separation rule or its face pin; both ends of an outer self-loop take the face of its state that the fewest other ends use.
    2. Reface (glyphs): when an arrival and a departure want one midpoint, move the one with more to gain to another face.
    3. Align: put both ends of a net between parallel faces on one coordinate, so one straight segment fits; a net with label room reserved takes the low end, and corridor nets are skipped.
    4. Spread: split ends sharing a point by direction of travel, a line of text apart where the face has room, else closer; repeat until nothing moves.
    5. Separate: push apart legs on different boxes that run closer than a line of text (fans exempt).
    6. Loop: put an outer self-loop's two ends a line of text apart about the middle of the widest run of its face that no other seat stands in.

    Nudging lanes apart

    Nudging spreads routes that run alongside each other, per frame and again over the whole chart.

    • A lane is a group of overlapping parallel segments closer than one em (192).
    • Within a lane, segments are ordered by where they came from, and reordered where that avoids a crossing; fan-ins and fan-outs move as one bundle.
    • Segments spread up to one em apart, within the room their frame and obstacles leave.
    • A move is kept only if it creates no collapsed leg, no new overlap with a box or its bumper, no new run along a border and no new shared run; otherwise the bundle stays put. A drawing that overlaps a box is worse than any score.

    Trims and failures

    PathClear shortens each route's first and last legs for arrowheads, by at most half the leg. A net fails if an end lies outside its region, if the frame's grid is too large, or if it is unreachable even with zero clearance. A failed net is drawn as a straight line with a RouteDegraded diagnostic.

    Only unreachable nets trigger the inflation retry, since the others do not depend on spacing: rank_sep, node_sep and sub_sep grow by 32 units on a copy of the profile and sizing and routing rerun, up to 8 times, keeping the least-degraded attempt. The cost is still scored under the caller's profile, and the search never accepts an inflated candidate: fitting only after widening everything is a bigger drawing, not a better one.

    One end, four faces

    The figure lays out estop with each face pinned in turn, each a full rerun of ordering, sizing and routing.

    RejectedPricing closeness instead of a bumper (needs a constant tuned against the bend penalty); a whole-em clearance (cost containment); congestion-aware routing (nothing measured needs it yet). The router is swappable by name.
    Phase 3, last step

    Labels: measured, anchored, placed

    A label is a box the application measured; layout hangs it off its own route, inside the state holding both ends, clear of everything else.

    Measured with scav's metrics

    The application measures text with scav's own metrics, so measuring, building and rendering never disagree.

    • Widths are summed in integers and rounded up, never to nearest, so a box is never smaller than its text.
    • Heights are the font size times a fixed ratio (269 units for 12 pt), not the font's own vertical metrics, which disagree with each other.
    • Kerning is ignored (erring wide), a missing glyph is an error, and there is one bundled font.
    • Layout never re-wraps a label, so height, width and placement need no fixpoint.

    A label's size is an input to ordering and sizing, which reserve room for it; its position is decided last, once every route is final. Both belong to the transition's LCA segment.

    The anchored model

    The box hangs off a point on its own route by an invisible leader half an em long (96 units). Candidates are every combination of:

    • a leg of the route inside the LCA frame,
    • a slide position along it, every half box height, ends included,
    • a leader direction (up, down, left, right),
    • one of eight attachment points on the box: side midpoints first (so ties centre the box on its leg), then corners.
    RulesEvery candidate lies inside its holder (the states enclosing both ends), is not cut by its own route, and avoids the states its route leaves and enters. The strict tier also avoids every other state, band, placed box and route; touching is not overlapping.

    The winner is the lexicographic minimum of (shortfall, dist, leg, attach, lead, slide):

    • shortfall, max(0, gap to own leg + h − gap to nearest foreign leg): a box nearer a neighbour's line than its own would read as the neighbour's label.
    • dist: distance from the box's centre to the anchor, the midpoint of the route's longest horizontal leg (else its longest leg).

    If no candidate passes the strict tier, the best loose one wins: it keeps the basic rules but may overlap. If nothing passes at all, the box is centred on the anchor and counted as unplaced. Several boxes on one transition are placed in order along the route. Candidates are pruned by the strict tier's bound; pruning by the loose one pushed boxes into the fallback. The boxes of a loop inside its state are not searched: they stack beside the loop's far leg, in room reserved for them.

    Labels in the cost

    A label over a foreign state or another route is Tier 0, forbidden rather than priced. If one endpoint encloses the other, or the transition is a loop inside its state, the label lives inside that state and only its bands count. A label over another label or an enclosing state's bands is Tier 2 (label), as is the shortfall (label_near).

    RejectedBoxes on fixed strips beside the line (they drifted far from their leg); rip-up-and-reroute (the loose tier made it unnecessary); "nothing between a label and its line" as a hard rule (many more fallbacks, no gain).
    Phases 2 and 3

    Decorated states: headers, bands and loops

    What an application draws inside a state is reserved before layout runs, and layout keeps every route, port and label out of it.

    Headers and bands

    The reference builder draws a PlantUML-style header at the top of each state: the name, centred; then, on a state with a description or a live region, a rule from border to border with the description under it. It reserves exactly the header's height.

    A band is interior room a state's BoxSpace reserves around its submachine area: h_before above, h_after below, and w_before and w_after before and after it, between the other two. Layout returns each as a rect (state_before, state_after, state_lead, state_trail) for the application to draw in, and the box formula adds all four. A header is an h_before band.

    RuleEvery band is an obstacle, because an application reserves room only for what it draws there. No route enters a band, no label overlaps one, and no port sits on a face a band lines. As walls, the side bands run from the top band's top to the bottom band's bottom, so no seam opens where two bands meet. A route may still end on a lined face: an arrow to the state itself touches its border and enters nothing.

    A state's bands and loop room are walls in every frame inside it that they overlap, so a route inside a headed composite goes round the header as it goes round a child, and nudging keeps lanes out of them. A route that enters one anyway is counted by Tier 0's through_band.

    Ports keep off lined faces

    A face is lined when a band covers it: the top by h_before, the bottom by h_after, the left by w_before and the right by w_after. A route crossing a composite's border does so at a port, and from a port on a lined face it would have to cross the band to reach the child. Since the reference builder heads every state, a route never enters a composite through its top.

    This holds by construction, not by price:

    • The facing pass never turns a port onto a lined face, and moves a port off one: to the opposite border if that is not lined, else to a top or bottom border that the child it joins can see past its siblings.
    • The search never offers a lined face as a side move.
    • If none of those is free, the request cannot be met. The port keeps its face, its route crosses the band, through_band counts the crossing, and layout still succeeds; the router draws that leg as its straight-line fallback.

    Loops inside a state

    An internal or local self-transition is a loop inside its source. It leaves the source's right border from inside, runs in to its far leg beside the label, and returns lower down with its arrowhead on the border. Each such loop takes one row of the state's loop room, which is reserved below the submachine area and right-aligned. A row is as tall as the loop's labels, and at least a lane plus a route clearance on each side.

    The loop room is sized from the loops' PathBoxes alone, so phase 3 and the cost re-derive it and no geometry column carries it. Phase 3 draws each loop in its row instead of routing it, and the room is a wall for every other route. The label is not searched: it sits beside the loop, inside the state and below its header.

    Loops outside a state

    An external self-transition is a net whose two ends name its state. The attach pass seats both ends on the face of the state that the fewest other ends use, the right face on a tie; the loop pass then puts them a line of text apart about the middle of the widest stretch of that face no other seat stands in. The route runs out 2·pad from each seat and back. A face pin may move either end, so the search can take a loop round a corner.

    Every transition is internal to its lowest common ancestor

    A route never crosses the border of the state that holds both its ends: it is drawn inside that state, through a port on each state between. A transition's kind only sets the default. Between two states of one machine a transition is external to each of them; one leaving a machine is internal to the composite holding both ends. An internal self-transition is the case where that composite is the state itself, so it is drawn inside it like any other.

    An internal transition from a composite into its own child starts on the composite's border, level with the boundary node ordering placed for it, unless another region of the composite lies between.

    What scav optimises

    The objective: three tiers, compared in order

    Every candidate drawing gets one Cost, and the search keeps the least, so the cost defines what "better" means.

    A cost is a triple (t0, t1, t2) compared lexicographically: lower t0 wins outright, then t1, then t2. There are no multipliers between tiers, because a huge weight inside one sum is a cliff that breaks local search and can overflow. Cost reads only the finished geometry. Touching never counts as overlapping, and segments cross only properly, not at a shared endpoint.

    Tier 0: forbidden, not priced

    t0 counts things a reader must never see; one outweighs any Tier 2 total. Most are impossible by construction, so Tier 0 is a safety net for degraded routes, trial drawings and label fallbacks. Every shipped example has t0 = 0.

    countforbids
    through_boxa route entering a state that neither encloses nor is one of its ends
    through_banda route entering a band of a state it may occupy, including the seam where two bands meet
    box_overlapsibling states overlapping
    vanisheda transition that should be drawn but has no route (else every Tier 2 term would score it perfect)
    flusha route running along a state's border, within 47 units
    through_regiona route entering a concurrent region neither end lies in
    retracea route turning straight back along itself
    label_over_boxa label over a state, except those enclosing both ends and the host (an endpoint enclosing the other, or the state a loop is drawn inside), whose bands count instead
    label_over_routea label over another transition's route

    Tier 1: hints

    t1 is reserved for author's layout hints, which are not built; it is always 0.

    Tier 2: thirteen weighted terms

    t2 is an integer sum. Each term is converted to a unit first: counts stay counts, lengths are divided by the em (the font size, 192 units on readable) and areas by em², rounding up. Then it is multiplied by its weight.

    termchargesunitweight
    bendseach change of directioncount512
    corridorlength two transitions share on one line, except the final leg into a common target (the trunk)em48
    crossingseach crossing between transitionscount512
    excess_lenroute length beyond its chord or label width, times (1 + its crossings)em4
    adjacencya transition joining two non-adjacent regions (fork and join exempt)count16
    labeloverlapping label pairs, and a label over an enclosing state's bandscount768
    label_neara label's shortfall: nearer a foreign leg than its ownem48
    aspectthe chart's distance from 16:10, |w·10 − h·16|em2
    areathe chart's w × hem²1
    crowdingparallel segments of different transitions closer than an em, falling linearly to zero at one emem512
    lengthtotal route lengthem8
    transit_bendsbends inside a state the route only passes through, on top of bendscount768
    whitespaceempty interior of composites (measured, unweighted)em²0

    Weights are capped at 1,024, which keeps the sum inside 64 bits.

    Weights are exchange rates

    With every term in its own unit, a weight says how much of one defect a reader would trade for another. On readable, one bend costs the same as one crossing, one em of crowded lanes, 64 em of route length, or 512 em² of canvas. Without the unit conversion, area (degree 2 in the coordinates) swamped every other term. The weights were then fitted to pick the drawing with the fewest defects a reader counts.

    Shares

    Each term's share of t2, in basis points, is committed per chart beside the cost goldens, so a reviewer sees what a weight change bought and sold.

    RejectedScoring per frame (routes leave their frame); a heavy excess_len (it rewards sprawl); a term rewarding routes for running together (the optimiser stacks them); a higher weight ceiling (the ceiling keeps the sum in 64 bits).
    How a drawing is found

    The search: rows, moves and kicks

    scav lays a chart out many thousands of times with slightly different inputs and ships the cheapest drawing; the search is deterministic throughout.

    A drawing is a pure function of (row, pins). A row is one setting of four whole-chart sizing knobs. A pin is one recorded decision the phases must honour; there are seven kinds: rank, cut, reverse, face, orient, side and fold. Pins are inputs, not patches, so trying a move means laying out again with one more pin and undoing it means dropping the pin: no transactions, no rollback. Pins name states and transitions by id, because node indices change between layouts.

    This makes every drawing a reproducible counterfactual: scav dump --layout prints a drawing's row and pins as flags, and --no-search with those flags redraws it exactly. Edit one flag to get the drawing a reader wants and score it: if it is cheaper, the search lacks a move; if dearer, the objective is wrong.

    Level 2: sixteen rows

    Level 2 is a fixed table of 16 rows; row i flips the knobs named by i's set bits. Row 0 is the profile as given, and the run fails if it is not viable. Every row is scored under the caller's profile, so all compare on one scale.

    bitknobwhat it changes
    0box packerwhether packing also tries the one-row box packer
    1compactionwhether LR-rectpacking compacts
    2ratio sourceeach frame packs toward 16:10, or toward its owner's interior
    3foldfold where the scale measure prefers, or wherever a run is long

    Every viable row is searched to convergence, and the cheapest result ships (ties to the lower row). Picking by starting cost would be wrong: on bottler, the row with the best start finishes 51% dearer than row 0.

    Level 1: steepest descent over pins

    The incumbent is the current best (row, pins). Each round lays out every move the incumbent allows, each a candidate with one more pin, in parallel; it takes the single best strictly improving move (ties to the earliest) and repeats until nothing improves. A candidate that is not viable or needed the inflation retry is never taken.

    moveoffered forwhy it exists
    cuteach chained segmentchained edges carry most kinks
    reverseeach cyclic segment not yet pinnedwhich edge breaks a cycle decides ranks
    faceeach end of a transition that bends or is charged a crossing, corridor, crowding, excess or label term (every end while Tier 0 is broken), × 4 facesa local face rule cannot see the turn it buys
    sideeach port end, × the other 3 sidesa route arriving from above can enter from above
    rankeach non-initial state, × every other rank in its framewhich column a state sits in; the largest source of gain
    fold (refold only)each folded framewhere the single fold cut falls

    Each move kind has its own budget of 1,024 scored moves over the whole search, so no kind starves another. A face move that cannot move its seat is charged but not scored.

    Kicks: iterated local search

    Greedy descent stops in the first basin it finds, and some structural changes pay off only after the search adapts to them. A kick applies one, searches to convergence, and keeps the result only if the converged cost is cheaper; unlike simulated annealing, there is no temperature to tune.

    • Kinds: reverse a cyclic segment; turn a frame to run down; flip whether a frame is folded. Turns and folds are allowed only in rounds "with turns".
    • Warm start: the incumbent's pins minus the kicked frame's own rank, cut, face, side and fold pins, plus the kick's pin, then Level 1 scoped to that frame. A round's kicks run in parallel.
    • Reduction: take each frame's best improving kick. If several frames have one, try them together; if that loses to the best single kick, take the single and rest each other winner on top, keeping it if it still improves. Repeat until no kick improves, then one unscoped settle search.
    • Two schedules run from each row: A allows turns from the start; B runs reversals alone first. B is kept only if strictly cheaper; neither dominates.
    • Rows whose converged drawings are identical kick only once.

    Refold and the search memo

    A final refold search runs Level 1 again from each row's pins with fold-cut moves added, kept only if strictly cheaper. A Level 1 search is a function of its inputs, so the search memo stores whole searches by those inputs and replays a repeated one from its result. Level 1 provides most of the gain and kicks most of the CPU time.

    RejectedIn-rank swaps (layered crossings are already zero); screening rows by a short search (it dropped the best row); turns and folds as greedy moves (worse basins); kick shortcuts such as depth caps (each lost quality); a frame-mirror move; sound lower bounds (neighbours are near-ties, see making it fast); random restarts (far worse per CPU second).
    Speed without changing a drawing

    Making the search fast, exactly

    Every optimisation here is exact: with or without it, every drawing is byte-identical.

    RuleEach optimisation has a test mode that runs the unoptimised computation alongside and compares, with a planted defect proving the comparison can fail.

    Every optimisation exploits one fact: a candidate is the incumbent plus one pin, so almost everything it computes has been computed before. Before them, one bottler layout ran Brandes–Köpf 19.8 million times for 69,496 distinct graphs. A general lower bound does not help, because most losing candidates land within 1% of the incumbent; the label bound below works because it bounds only the label half of the cost.

    Frame memos

    Each thread keeps four memos, each keyed on everything its step reads: Brandes–Köpf by the whole graph, each frame's ordering and sizing by that frame's inputs and pins, and each label's placement by its box, route and nearby obstacles. Keys are interned, so a frame is named by a serial number rather than spelled out. Each memo is capped at 4 MiB per thread. Traced runs bypass the ordering and sizing memos.

    Ordering and sizing reuse

    Even a memo hit builds and hashes a key; reuse skips that. An ordering records what each frame read beyond the graph (its pins, label charges, orientation and the profile). A candidate compares those records with the incumbent's, orders only the frames that differ, and copies the rest. Sizing does the same, except that a frame's size depends on its children's, so every frame holding a changed one is re-sized too. Most frames are copied.

    The face shortcut

    Ordering, sizing and the facing pass never read a face pin, so a face candidate starts from the incumbent's sizing and only routes and scores, at about a quarter of the cost; it also keeps every label nothing it reads has changed. A face that would not move its seat draws the incumbent exactly, so it is charged but not scored, and faces are offered only where the move table says they are priced.

    The label bound

    Labels are placed last and read only the routes, so a round with labels runs in two passes:

    1. Route every candidate without labels and score a lower bound: label terms are zero, and area is measured on the unlabelled chart.
    2. Visit candidates whose bound beats the incumbent, least bound first. Label and score each exactly while its bound can still beat the best so far; stop at the first that cannot.

    The pick is exactly what scoring every candidate whole would give, and most candidates never place their labels. The 128 most promising candidates keep their routes from the first pass, so their exact pass does not route again.

    Smaller wins

    • No allocation: every stage fills per-thread buffers reused across candidates; ordering keeps one per nesting depth, because a waiting thread may run a nested candidate.
    • Radix A* queue: A* pops in a strict total order, so any exact priority queue gives the same sequence; a radix heap is faster.
    • Integer square root by Newton's method from above, checked exhaustively over all 32-bit inputs.
    • One global pool: nested work (rows, searches, candidate rounds) shares one pool, so no call site divides the cores among its children, and the search memo removes repeated searches.
    RejectedDepth caps and early abandonment of kicks; budgets that shrink with chart size, since searching a big chart less concedes the goal.
    Proof it holds

    Determinism: goldens, hashes and selftest

    Three hashes per drawing, committed goldens and a self-test check that the same inputs give the same bytes on every machine.

    Three hashes

    Every laid-out chart carries three 32-bit xxHash32 digests, computed byte by byte so every machine agrees:

    • Inputs digest: everything that is not geometry (the profile, the router, the packer choice, the space requests). A golden is reproducible only against a stated measurement policy, and this names it.
    • Structural hash: ranks, in-rank orders, port sides and each route's turns, seeded with the model. Ranks are recovered from the rectangles, so it can be recomputed from a finished drawing.
    • Coordinate hash: every rectangle, point and port.

    The split localises a change: moving the drawing changes only the coordinate hash, and remeasuring text without reordering changes only the inputs digest and coordinates.

    Selftest and thread counts

    scav selftest lays every built-in chart out at 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 and 16 threads and compares all three hashes with the embedded goldens. A difference from the golden is a toolchain finding; a difference between thread counts is a sharding defect, since the shards and their merge order never depend on the schedule.

    The determinism test compares every geometry column's bytes, the hashes and the chosen Level 2 row across those thread counts, under a delay injector that reshuffles the schedule. It includes the inflation retry and a chart where every row ties, so index-ordered merging decides. Timing never gates a determinism claim.

    CI runs six toolchains (clang, gcc and MSVC, on macOS, Linux and Windows) × Debug, Release and a testable build × the thread counts. Odd and prime thread counts are mandatory, because they expose merge-order bugs that powers of two hide. The testable build must match Release byte for byte; with integer arithmetic, any divergence means undefined behaviour.

    Goldens

    Committed goldens hold the three hashes, every cost term at both scales, the shares, every router's results, and draw-list, dump and SVG output.

    How scav is tested

    • Unit tests type inputs in as plain structs: no disk, no parsing, no earlier stage, so a defect fails one test, not a hash three stages away.
    • The gauntlet: 31 one-element charts, small enough to name every route, held to reader-visible properties (no route through a box, every route axis-aligned and reaching its ends) on what actually ships. A property that does not hold yet is carved out with a pinned count.
    • Every rule gets an isolated test on a trivial layout, every fixed bug leaves a test, and every optimisation has a test mode.
    • Also golden, property, sanitizer, fuzz, Python binding and baseline tests. Performance tests assert floors, never times.

    The trace lists layout's decisions (rank assigned, edge reversed, candidate scored and so on). It forces one thread and replays the winning (row, pins), and traced runs hash the same as untraced ones. The figures marked "from the trace" read it.

    Reference

    Glossary

    Every term on this page in one line, linked to the section that explains it.

    Anchor (label)
    Midpoint of a route's longest horizontal leg; labels are pulled toward it. → labels
    Attachment point
    One of eight points on a label box where its leader ends. → labels
    Band
    Room a state reserves around its submachine area (h_before, h_after, w_before, w_after); every band is an obstacle. → decorated states
    Bend
    A route vertex where the direction changes; 512 in Tier 2. → cost

    A dummy node chaining a long edge through an intermediate rank; a routing waypoint. → order

    The router's cost per turn: one rank_sep (576). → route

    A port's node on its frame's edge: exits trailing, entries leading. → decompose
    BoxSpace
    Per state and submachine: text width and four bands around its children. → intro
    Brandes–Köpf (BK)
    Linear-time, balanced placement of nodes across the ranks. → size
    Candidate
    One pass from ordering through cost for one row and set of pins. → pipeline

    The router's bumper around boxes: node_sep / 3 = 96 units. → route

    The objective: forbidden counts, then hints, then weighted terms, compared in order. → cost

    Desired aspect ratio: 16:10 on readable. → size
